The GPU, NPU and CPU settings therefore already equal the vendor's, so applying the vendor QoS values cannot move this result. Question: does the loss shrink once each job amortizes its latency-bound phases? Stage 1b ran small jobs with both devices together. The jobs were a 65-element GPU add (about 100 us, almost all per-job work) and a 16x176 int16 relu (11,264 bytes, 5.6 us). Against the phase with no streaming, they lost: - core 2: GPU 25.4%, NPU 11.4%; - core 7: GPU 32.5%, NPU 29.3%; - cores 2-4: GPU 51.1%, NPU 48.1%; - cores 2-5 and 7: GPU 51.1%, NPU 53.0%.  Data (no board run): - Neither device overlaps its own jobs. Four GPU jobs in flight ran at the serial rate (102.8 us serial, 104.6 us pipelined), and the NPU stays busy at depth 8. A deeper queue cannot help; only the work inside each job can change. - The relu job moves 2.0 GB/s with no streaming, far below the DRAM ceiling, so its own accesses wait on latency. Whether a large transfer keeps enough requests in flight to hide the loaded latency is the open question. - The large relu is compiled. tools/npu-graph-build.py built a 1024x176 int16 relu in the pinned compiler container. Its network binary is the same 5,832 bytes as the stage-1b relu and differs in 22 bytes, all dimension and size fields. The compiler emits the same single operation with 64 times the tensor and does not split it into several operations. - Cache maintenance per job. The NPU invalidates outputs only at acquire. The GPU cleans and invalidates each binding's sync range at completion. Its conflict check (drivers/gpu/pvr_compute_fast.c, conflicts) compares only GPU-write leases, so an input binding with no sync range never conflicts. - GPU leases larger than one page pass admission: platform/a733/gpu_queue.c rounds a lease to its block, identity-maps it and maps it in data pages of up to 256 KiB (BRN 71317). Every GPU lease run on the board so far is 4 KiB, so this run is their first board use.  Build: the accel-overlap sweep with larger jobs, in work/concurrent-accel-1c-1114. - GPU: 262,144-element adds (8,192 workgroups of 32; the program bounds work items by the count). Each job reads 2 MiB of inputs and writes 1 MiB into its own slot of a 4 MiB output region. Inputs are written and cleaned once.   - Deviation for approval: pipelined jobs name one 64-byte sync line per slot. The conflict check then sees four distinct slots, and the queue maintains 64 bytes per job; the GPU MMU confines the program to the lease, not to the range. Output cache maintenance is therefore not part of the measured job.   - After each phase's pipelined second, one serial job per slot runs with the full 1 MiB sync range, and its whole output is compared with the arithmetic result. - NPU: the 1024x176 relu (360,448 bytes in and out), with its simulator reference. The last output of each phase is compared in full. - Both devices run together, as in stage 1b, so stage 1b's losses are a like-for-like comparison. - Deviation for approval: two control phases run each device alone with no streaming. Two large-job devices could slow each other, which would lower the no-streaming baseline and hide part of the CPU's effect. - Nine phases of 1 s, with the dependent-load chase on core 0 in every phase:   0. GPU alone, no streaming;   1. NPU alone, no streaming;   2. both, no streaming (the baseline);   3. both, core 2;   4. both, core 7;   5. both, cores 2-4;   6. both, cores 2-5 and 7 (the stage-1 set);   7. both, core 2 running three interleaved sequential streams over three 4 MiB areas in one loop;   8. both, the same on core 7. - Deviation for approval: phases 7 and 8 are new streaming sets. - Regions: GPU input 2 MiB, GPU output 4 MiB, stream 36 MiB, chase 16 MiB. The vectors input grows by about 0.7 MB. - The main task's progress call becomes time-based, because a slow large job must not stretch the 1 s progress window. The decoder takes the nine phases and the minimum job counts below.  Predictions. Losses are against phase 2. - Rates with no streaming:   - GPU alone 300-2,000 jobs/s (3 MiB per job at 3-8 GB/s plus 0.1 ms; the program loads one 4-byte word per work item);   - NPU alone 4,000-11,000 jobs/s (0.72 MB per job at 3-8 GB/s);   - in phase 2, each device at 80-100% of its alone rate. - My expectation is that the per-byte path is latency-bound as well, so a larger job loses about as much as a small one. Each streaming phase's large-job loss is within 15 points of the same device's stage-1b loss:   - core 2: GPU 10-40%, NPU 0-26%;   - core 7: GPU 18-48%, NPU 14-44%;   - cores 2-4: GPU 36-66%, NPU 33-63%;   - stage-1 set: GPU 36-66%, NPU 38-68%. - Interleaved streams: each of phases 7 and 8 costs each device within 10 points of the same core's single stream (phase 3 or 4). - Minimum counts: each device completes at least 200 pipelined jobs in every phase, and at least 200 NPU completions occur with a GPU job in flight in each phase of both devices. - Every checked output matches its reference. PLL_NPU stays unchanged and locked, no phase throttles, and the top point holds at the start and the end.  Decision rules: - Validity. If a device's phase-2 rate is below 80% of its alone rate, the devices slow each other. The comparison with stage 1b is then reported as confounded for that device. - Job structure, for each device at the stage-1 set:   - Lever: the loss is at most half its stage-1b loss (GPU at most 25.5%, NPU at most 26.5%). Larger jobs are the lever for that device. Next: shape real workloads, such as camera and lidar frames, into large jobs.   - Not a lever: the loss is within 15 points of stage 1b (GPU 36-66%, NPU 38-68%). CPU-side bounding is the lever. Next: read the AXI2HIF limiter words and CPU_DA_DDR_CTRL_REG (read only), and send a hypothesis for any write.   - Partial: any value in between (GPU 25.5-36%, NPU 26.5-38%). Larger jobs recover part of the loss. Next: one run at two more sizes (16 and 256 times) to find the size at which the loss stops falling, before choosing. - Stream count (one direction only):   - If three interleaved streams on one core cost within 10 points of that core's single stream, row interleaving does not set the loss, and the number of requesting cores does.   - A larger cost does not prove bank or row conflicts, because one core may keep more requests outstanding with three streams. The bandwidth of phases 7 and 8 against phases 3 and 4 is reported beside it.   - Core 2 is the sharper test: one stream there cost the NPU 11% in stage 1b, three streams on cores 2-4 cost 48%.  DRAM-controller counters that could separate outstanding-transaction limits from bank and row conflicts: - The DRAM controller has no documented counter. The A733 manual 11.1 (DRAMC, 0x0a020000 common and 0x0a100000 controller 0) lists features only and has no register chapter. Boot0 writes none of the scheduler or performance registers that a DesignWare uMCTL2 would place at 0x250-0x26c or 0x404 and above. Nothing local counts row hits, row misses or bank conflicts. - NSI performance counters exist for each master and for the DRAM-side target agent. Per port n, at 0x02020000 + 0x200*n:   - +0xc0 enable, +0xc4 clear, +0xc8 period in cycles;   - +0xcc/+0xd0 read and write requests;   - +0xd4/+0xd8 read and write data, in 16-byte units;   - +0xdc/+0xe0 read and write latency accumulators.   - On the A733, the GPU is port 6, the NPU 18, the CPU 19 and 20, and the target agent 32 (33 on a dual channel).   - Sources: the vendor kernel's bsp/drivers/bus/sunxi-nsi.h lines 377-385, and its sun60iw2 enum at lines 195-218; sunxi-nsi.c lines 740-790 for the period, clear and enable sequence. - AXI2HIF CPU counters exist at 0x0a030000 and 0x0a040000:   - +0x20 enable, +0x24 clear, +0x28 period;   - +0x80/+0x84 read and write requests, +0x88/+0x8c read and write data, +0x90/+0x94 read and write latency.   - Source: sunxi-nsi.h lines 394-411. The A733 takes the branch that excludes sun65iw1; the alternative offsets 0x98-0x104 apply to sun65iw1 only.   - CPU traffic does not pass the NSI, so these are the only CPU-side counts. - How they would separate the causes:   - The mean outstanding transactions of a master is the latency accumulator divided by the request count, times the request rate (Little's law).   - An outstanding-transaction limit would show as the CPU's outstanding count flattening at a constant while its latency grows with stream count, with the target agent's data rate flat.   - Bank and row conflicts would show as the delivered data rate falling as streams are added while outstanding counts rise. Stage 1b already shows the CPU total falling from 6.95 to 6.26 GB/s when cores 5 and 7 joined.   - No counter measures row hits directly, and the latency counter's units are unverified. - Both counter banks need writes (period, clear and enable), so stage 1c leaves them unused; the interleaved-stream phases are the write-free test. drivers/gpu/a733_gpu_nsi_pmu.c already implements the vendor sequence for port 6 behind SUNSTONE_GPU_NSI_PMU (host-tested; board calibration open). A later hypothesis could extend it to ports 18, 19, 20 and 32 and to the AXI2HIF counters. The run limit is 25 s inside the 60 s lifetime. - Readback and rail restore 9 s. - Total 55-70 s. conclusion: The larger-job sweep returned normally with every compared output equal to its reference, PLL_NPU unchanged and locked, no throttle and the top point held. Larger jobs lose more, not less: at the stage-1 streaming set the GPU lost 68.3% and the NPU 69.2% against both devices with no streaming, against 51.1% and 53.0% for stage 1b's small jobs. The large relu moves 7.3 GB/s alone (10,184 jobs/s of 721 kB), so it is bandwidth-bound and shares the DRAM total with the CPU: CPU streams plus accelerator traffic came to 7.2-8.8 GB/s in the single-area streaming phases and 6.5-6.7 GB/s in the interleaved ones, against 5.9 GB/s with no streaming. The two large-job devices also slow each other (GPU 64.7% and NPU 74.2% of their alone rates), so the comparison with stage 1b is confounded by the validity rule; against the alone rates the losses at the stage-1 set are 79% (GPU) and 77% (NPU). Three interleaved streams on one core cost within 6 points of that core's single stream while moving 35-38% fewer bytes (core 2: 2.38 against 3.86 GB/s), so the loss follows the requesting core, not row interleaving or bytes. One A55 core streaming 2.4 GB/s cost both large-job devices 30%. Output cache maintenance of a full 1 MiB slot added 20-142 us to a 4.5-12.6 ms GPU job, within the job-to-job variation. The GPU add moves only 0.7 GB/s alone (4.48 ms per job), since each work item loads one 4-byte word.
